notes.text: Morocco has no binding loan-to-value cap: a 2008 ethics code agreed between Bank Al-Maghrib and banks only guides LTVs below 100%. In 2024 new housing loans had an average LTV of about 84%, with 41% originated at 90% to 100% and about 8% above 100%, and the IMF has recommended binding, more conservative caps once a borrower-level database is completed by end-2026, which would tighten access to credit for buyers with small deposits.

sources.title: Morocco: 2026 Article IV Consultation and Review under the Flexible Credit Line Arrangement, Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/72)

notes.text: Supported by infrastructure projects and lower interest rates, credit grew 8% year on year in December 2025, with mortgage and consumer lending among the drivers, while non-performing loans to households rose as inflation and drought squeezed incomes. Easier credit supports housing demand, but rising household arrears limit how far lending can expand.

notes.text: In January 2024 Morocco switched its housing support from the supply side, through tax incentives and exemptions for developers, to direct cash aid to buyers allocated first come, first served through a digital process; about 28,262 households had benefited by December 2024, and the housing ministry earmarked about MAD 3.6 billion for housing aid in 2025. Demand-side grants raise buyers' purchasing power and support prices in the eligible segments.
